paragraphs: "Dammit!" Charlie growls, struggling to fold an impractically large map over your car's steering wheel and avoid veering offroad into a tree at the same time.
"Can you just let me hold the map?" you ask. "No. I can do this just fine," Charlie says, then slams on the brakes to round another tight bend.

It is late afternoon on a rural backroad deep within the Black Hills of South Dakota. The sun is high, but the air is cold. You've seen nothing but pine trees and two narrow winding lanes for over an hour. Your car's radio is getting weaker. It splutters out a Neil Diamond song laced with static.
Check/tick Alex on the log sheet. To keep offering help, go to 7. To change the radio station instead, go to 3.

"Buzz…," Alex mutters absent-mindedly, opening and closing the car's electric window for the tenth time in two minutes. You grit your teeth. You only just got back on the road after your truck stop break, and Alex has already fiddled with every button within reach. You're left to steer the car and navigate using a ridiculously oversized map. Alex gets bored of the window, sighs, then turns to you. "Can you just let me hold the map?"
"No. I can do this just fine," you reply. The two of you already missed one turnoff this trip because Alex lost track of your route. It's better for you to just take care of everything.

It is late afternoon on a rural backroad deep within the Black Hills. The sun is high, but the air is cold. Tall pine trees and rolling valleys stretch as far as you can see in every direction. Crisp autumn air drifts in through Alex's open window. Then, you hear an electronic buzz for a moment. Suddenly it appears again. On and off. On and off. You bite your tongue and keep silent. Alex turns on the radio. You hear a harsh screech of static as they start scanning through different frequencies. This is all pointless. You're way out of signal range. The only song you can pick up is a heavily distorted Neil Diamond single.
Check/tick Charlie on the log sheet. To ask Alex to stop, go to 83. To just ignore the sound, go to 96.
You reach forward and turn the dial. The speakers vomit static while you scan for a signal.
"Please," Charlie barks, and turns the radio off. "I can't think with all that noise."

You raise your hands defensively. "Sorry," you say, but Charlie ignores you. You stare at them for a few seconds, then sigh and turn to stare out the window. You watch the muddy green blur of passing trees for several minutes.
"Finally," Charlie says. They jab a finger down at the still tangled map. "It's the next left."
You peer ahead and spot a tiny unpaved road cutting deeper into the forest. Charlie pulls onto it and the two of you weave through the trees in silence.
Make a Psychology roll to gauge how Charlie is feeling: • If you succeed the roll, go to 4. • If you fail the roll, go to 8.
Charlie seems agitated. It's been over three hours in the car, so that's understandable. You reach over, put a hand on their leg, and squeeze. You see them smile just a little in response.

"Not far now," Charlie says. "Good. I can't wait to stretch my legs." You continue deeper into the forest. The little road you're on winds erratically, dipping up and down as it dodges between hills. The sky gets lost in the branches of pine trees. As the evening shadows lengthen, you feel cold seeping in from outside.
Go to 5.

After a few minutes, a few more turns, and a few miles' travel deeper into the forest, the sun sets. Your car's headlights cut into the darkness, revealing the road ahead just a few feet at a time. Eventually, the lights drift over the front of a cabin, reflecting off two windows on either side of a front door, which seem to stare back at you, ominously.
The car stops and the headlights shut off. "Finally," you sigh, and step out onto the gravel driveway. As you walk
around to the trunk to help with the suitcases, the cold night air seizes around you like a vice.
"Are you hungry?" Charlie asks, while you try to keep from shivering.
Make a CON roll; if you fail, check/tick Touched by Cold on the log sheet.
To say you are hungry, go to 6. To say you aren't hungry, go to 12.
You nod. "Sure. Hamburgers?"

"Hamburgers it is." You take a brown grocery bag from the car's trunk, grab your suitcase, and walk to the cabin door. Charlie opens it up and steps inside. You follow, closing the door behind you to keep the chill out.
Go to 11.
"We're off of I-90, remember?" you say.
After a few moments of sulking, Charlie mutters a response, "I remember."

You reach over. "Here, lemme help with tha-" "No!" Charlie yanks the map away. "Alex, just let me, okay?" You put your hands up defensively and roll your eyes. Charlie drives on determinedly for a few more minutes before spotting a tiny unpaved road cutting deeper into the forest. Charlie pulls onto it, and the two of you weave through the trees in silence.
Make a Psychology roll to gauge how Charlie is feeling: • If you succeed the roll, go to 4. • If you fail the roll, go to 8.
Charlie's sulking. This vacation is turning out exactly like you thought it would. Charlie always insists on driving, gets lost,
and then refuses to ask for help. The weekend is shaping up to be a nightmare.

"Anyways," Charlie says, "it's not far now." Charlie drives deeper into the forest. The little road you're on winds erratically, dipping up and down as it weaves between hills. Above you, thick gray clouds obscure the sunlight. Soon, the sky gets lost in the branches of pine trees. You feel the cold seeping in from outside.
Go to 5.

You land a solid blow, right against the monster's face. The face it stole from your partner. Your strike splits the flesh, and it rips away into nothingness. The creature itself is completely unharmed. How could you possibly hurt it? It is an erupting mutating beast. But, in the one moment you strike it, you take back some measure of control. You rip away your partner's face from it. That simple gesture is enough to make your heart surge with righteous victory. This thing can't take everything from you.

You don't hold the beast back for long. It grabs at you with a tentacle that comes whipping at your side. As the tentacles boil and writhe before you, an alien voice resonates in the forest around you.
"This is your last chance. Accept the Child and be born anew, or reject it, and suffer."
To accept, go to 27. To refuse, go to 134. If Temporal Steel is checked/ticked on the log sheet, and Knife to a Gun Fight is not checked/ticked on the log sheet, go to 363.

No. No! You race for the edge of the clearing. You can make it out if you're fast enough! You hear the warped sound of your partner's voice calling after you but don't turn to look back. Then, you hear heavy slamming footsteps approaching fast. You can't help but look back for a moment. You see that your partner's body has warped and deformed. Their skin has split, and horrid dark branches burst from their flesh. Propelled by those disgusting long tendrils, they surge forward toward you. You turn back and race for the tree line. If you can just get there and break free, you can leave all this behind you!
Make a DEX roll: If you succeed, go to 360. If you fail, go to 359.

The cabin isn't very big; it's just one central room with a double bed, a chest of drawers, and a corner set up to serve as a kitchen. There's no microwave; both the oven and stove use gas. You see two doors: one goes to the rear of the cabin while another leads to a small bathroom. You just know it's going to be freezing in there.
On the wall opposite the bed is a TV and VCR unit sitting on top of a cupboard. The whole cabin is lit by muted yellow bulbs. It's not dark but it's not quite light either.
"I'll be in the john," Charlie says, then steps inside the small bathroom and shuts the door. You are left alone.

You put your suitcase on the bed, take out a few essentials, then move to the kitchen and unpack your groceries. There is a gas fridge and icebox that, judging by the steady and not-at-all-soft hum emanating from it, was installed sometime in the 1970s.
To get started on dinner, go to 13. To wait for Charlie, go to 16.
"Not especially," you say.

"All right, let's eat soon though. I'm starved." You take a brown grocery bag from the car's trunk, grab your suitcase, and walk to the cabin door. Charlie opens it up and steps inside. You follow, closing the door behind you to keep the chill out.
Go to 11.
You unpack ingredients for hamburgers. You find matches in a drawer, hold a lit one to the stove's gas burner, and turn the dial. Nothing happens.
"Damn thing." You ignore the front-left burner and use the front-right instead. It lights up super quick.
You've got patties frying and are chopping tomatoes when you hear the toilet flush. Charlie emerges from the bathroom soon after, sighing contentedly.
"Woof… sorry. I've been holding onto that one since we left Pierre."

"How charming," you mutter. Charlie comes up behind you and wraps their arms around your waist. You feel their breath on your neck, then the brush of a kiss against your cheek. "I love you," Charlie whispers.
To respond lovingly, go to 14. To change the subject, go to 17.
"I love you, too." You turn your head toward Charlie and kiss back. "Now scoot! I need to finish dinner."
You busy yourself in the kitchen while Charlie flops onto the bed. "I'm so glad we're here."

"Me too." "I think it'll be really good for us; you know?" "Yeah." "Like Doctor O'Brien told us," Charlie says, staring at the cabin's warped reflection in the mirror black TV screen, "getting away from everything to just focus on us will be great. I think it could be really healing…"
To talk about plans for tomorrow, go to 18. To reassure Charlie, go to 15.
"Yeah," you say with a faint smile. "It'll be great. I know it."

A few minutes pass, then you serve up the burgers. You and Charlie sit and eat silently. You find the cabin's nearby window strange. Outside it's so dark that all you can see is your own reflection. It's like looking into a mirror.

"What do you wanna do tonight?" you ask, mouth half-full. Charlie raises an eyebrow. You roll your eyes. "Seriously." "Well, you wanna go on a hike tomorrow, right?" You nod. "How about we just fire up a movie and take it easy?" Charlie gestures at the TV.
To agree, go to 19. To complain, go to 25.

There's a little round table in the corner of the kitchen. You sit at it and rest your head in your hands. You wonder how much Mark—Charlie's brother—paid for this place, and whether it had been worth it considering he's never out here. You also wonder if the cabin fixed his marriage like it's supposed to be helping you and Charlie's relationship. Somehow, you doubt it.
Charlie emerges from the bathroom, sighing contentedly. "Woof… sorry. I've been holding onto that one since we left Pierre."

"How charming," you mutter. Charlie comes up behind you and wraps their arms around your waist. You feel their breath on your neck, then the brush of a kiss against your cheek. "I love you," Charlie whispers.
To respond lovingly, go to 14. To change the subject, go to 17.
"How do you want your burger?"
"Erm. Medium, I guess." "Okay. Thanks." You stay in the kitchen. Charlie hovers uncertainly for a moment, then walks away and flops down on the bed. "I'm so glad we're here."

"Me too." "I think it'll be really good for us; you know?" "Yeah." "Like Doctor O'Brien told us," Charlie says, staring at the cabin's warped reflection in the mirror black TV screen, "getting away from everything to just focus on us will be great. I think it could be really healing…"
Check/tick Broken Heart on the log sheet. To talk about plans for tomorrow, go to 18. To reassure Charlie, go to 15.
"You still wanna go on a hike with me tomorrow?"

Charlie chuckles. "Yeah, sure. I mean, what else we gonna do, right?" Their laughter hangs awkwardly in the air for a moment. Then Charlie coughs and quickly changes tone. "It's beautiful here though, really."
"Yeah." "I can't wait to see the sunrise." After a few minutes, you serve up the burgers. Dinner passes in near total silence.
"What about tonight though?" Charlie asks. You swallow your last mouthful of food. "What about it?" "It's been a long day. How about we catch a flick?" Charlie gestures at the TV.
To agree, go to 19. To complain, go to 25.
"Sure," you say.
Charlie grins, then takes the dishes and heads over to the sink to clean them. You walk over to the TV unit.

It's a relatively cheap model from the late 1980s sitting on top of a dusty VCR player. You switch both on and open a cabinet beneath them, wondering what videos Charlie's brother and his wife left behind.

"He sure likes scary movies," you say, looking over the titles. Fifteen different tapes, and you're sure that covers pretty much every major slasher film of the last decade. "God, none of these looks good."
"There's not even a single comedy?" Charlie asks from the kitchen.
Make a Spot Hidden roll: • If you succeed the roll, go to 26. • If you fail the roll, go to 20.
You take out the tapes and go through them one by one, rolling your eyes and performatively gagging at each cover as you go.
Charlie walks over and joins you. "Maybe we should have stopped by a Blockbuster on the way."
"You're telling me. These covers all look cheap. Think they're bootlegged?"
"Probably." Charlie shrugs. "I could have sworn he said there was more than just horror. He said they watched something that sounded like a chick flick last time they came up."
"Maybe it's still in the VCR?" Charlie leans over and presses the eject button on the machine. There is a whirring of mechanical internals then the unit spits out a tape.
"Ah-hah!" Charlie says. "Is it blank?" you ask. "Nothing written on it. But they're bootlegs, right?" You shrug. "Whatever. Rewind it and we'll take our chances. It can't be worse than any of these."
To watch the movie right away, go to 28. To get ready for bed first, go to 21.

You grab your bag with one hand and head for the bathroom. "I'll be right back," you say, and slip inside. It's even colder in the bathroom. You set the bag on the sink and blink at your reflection staring back at you from a nearby mirror.

The door creaks open just a little. You sigh and push it closed again but it doesn't take. You look closer and see a little latch at head height. The door obviously can't hold itself shut unless it's locked. You roll your eyes, ignore the door, and brush your teeth.
A few minutes later you return to the main room and change while Charlie waits patiently on the bed. The movie is all set up, paused at the beginning. You climb up onto the bed and settle in as well.
"Ready for the random, hopefully-not-horror film?" Charlie asks.
"Sure am, start it up!" You smile and slip under the blankets. Charlie presses play on the remote.
Check/tick Occupied on the log sheet. Go to 22.
When the film begins, the screen is black. There is faint music but no opening credits. Then, the screen cuts to blurry footage that was clearly recorded on a hand-held camera.
"Is this one of Mark's home movies?" you ask. Charlie laughs then reaches for the remote. "Oh wow. I'm sorry."
"Wait a second, that looks familiar," you say, pointing at the TV. Charlie hesitates.

On screen, you see a wall of tall forest trees. Leaves and pine needles crunch under the feet of whoever's filming. The camera pans across the landscape, creating a blur of greens and browns. Suddenly, you spot Mark's cabin, standing alone in its little clearing. A dull red sedan is parked out front.

"That's Julie's car," Charlie says. "This must have been after their wedding." The camera is shaky. Wind rushes against the microphone, causing a brief flurry of horrid scraping from the speakers. There's movement near the red car. A woman, Julie, is taking bags from the trunk. She's smiling.
"Yeah," Charlie says. "This is at least five, six years ago."
Julie turns as the cabin door opens. Mark steps out, walks over, and takes one of the bags from her. They smile and exchange unheard words.

You sit bolt upright. "What the hell?" "What's wrong? It's only Mark." "Yeah, so who's filming?" Charlie stammers and blinks. On the screen, Mark and Julie go inside and close the door behind them. The camera zooms in toward the window. The picture is a grainy blur of colors. You see movement in the cabin. The camera zooms even closer. Then, harsh wind picks up and howls through the speakers. The image smashes to a slurry of loud static. White noise booms out into the room. The sound drills into your skull. You feel like it's going to make your head explode.
Make a note of this entry number, you may need to return to it. Make a Sanity roll; if you fail, lose 1 Sanity and check/tick Unsettled on the log sheet.
To cover your ears, go to 29. To scramble for the dial and turn it down, go to 23.
You dart from the bed, grimacing at the ear-splitting noise. You switch the dial and kill the TV.
Charlie is sitting on the bed with their hands clamped over their ears like a dope. "Sorry, it's only a remote for the VCR. There's no volume control."
"What the hell was that?" you ask angrily as you step away and slump back onto the bed.
Charlie shrugs. "I dunno." "Mark and Julie came out here with someone else?" Charlie laughs. "I don't really want to think about what my brother and his wife might get up to when they're out here."
You roll your eyes. "That was creepy. It was like a peeping Tom."
"Well, we know it's not." Charlie gestures to the TV cabinet. "Why would Mark and Julie have the tape?"
If Broken Heart is checked on the log sheet, you cannot stay calm. You must go to 24.
To get frustrated with Charlie, go to 24. To stay calm, go to 30.
You sigh. "Whatever. You always know best, right?"

Charlie frowns. "What's that supposed to mean?" You remember the car ride up. The way Charlie was reading the map while driving, refusing your help, and getting lost over and over. "Never mind," you say, then roll over in bed. "Can you get the light?"
"You don't want to watch a movie anymore?" "No," you say, and pull the blanket tight around yourself. "I just want to sleep."
Charlie sighs, "Fine." You feel the bed shift as they stand. "I just think that—"

The TV set blares to life again. It bellows static throughout the cabin. Thunderous scraping and coughing bounces off the walls. You thrash and cover your ears. Charlie swears but you can hardly hear it. The noise builds to a frenetic peak. It's almost unbearable. Then, just as quickly as it began, the noise stops and the TV falls silent. All the lights in the cabin go dead.
The power is out.
Check/tick Blame Game on the log sheet. Go to 31.
"Wow, I love to drive for five hours just to sit and watch TV like we do at home."

"Oh c'mon. It was a long drive. Let's relax. Here, let me." Charlie takes the finished dishes and starts cleaning up. "Julie and Mark came here a bunch. He said there's plenty of movies in the cabinet. You can pick whatever one you want. I'm sure you'll see something you love."

"Oh yeah?" you ask, skeptical. "I promise." Charlie nods toward the TV. "Go on." You get up and go and sit in front of the TV cabinet across from the bed. It's a relatively cheap unit from the late 80s sitting on top of a dusty VCR player. You switch both on, then open a cabinet beneath, looking for videos.

"Can't see anything but horror movies," you say, looking over the titles. Pretty much every major slasher film of the last decade. "None of these look any good. Unless you brought me here to murder me."
"No, there's got to be a comedy in there somewhere," Charlie says from the kitchen.
Make a Spot Hidden roll: • If you succeed the roll, go to 26. • If you fail the roll, go to 20.

As you're leafing through the tapes, you notice something at the back of the cabinet. You reach inside and pull it out. It's an empty slipcase for a VHS tape. It's flimsy. Someone has scrawled a title on it in black marker: The Flowers in the Stream.
You incredulously read the name aloud. "What's that?" Charlie says. "Empty case." Charlie walks over, wiping their wet hands on their pants. "I've never even heard of that movie."
"Should have stopped at Blockbuster," you mutter. "It looks like a bootleg. This is just the box though; I can't find the tape."
"Maybe it's still in the VCR?" Charlie leans over and presses the eject button. There is a whirring of internal mechanisms, then the unit spits out a tape.
"Ah-hah!" Charlie says. You nod. "Okay. Well, rewind it and we'll take our chances. It can't be worse than any of these." You gesture at the smattering of schlocky horror tapes.
Check/tick The Flowers in the Stream on the log sheet. To get changed before the movie, go to 21. To lay on the bed and watch it now, go to 28.
"I accept."

You sag as soon as you say the words. Dread washes over you, but so does a great sense of relief. After everything that's happened to you, all the exhausting things, it's relieving to just… let go. You put your misgivings to the side. Somehow, you know you're signing your death warrant, if not something worse, but at least you've done so willingly, and taken back some measure of control.

The creature before you moves slowly closer. It takes you toward it, delicately. Thousands of writhing tentacles begin to envelop you, obscuring your vision. Then, you feel a sharp, painful jab against your chest. A sharp tentacle has stabbed into your heart. You cough, involuntarily. Tiny droplets of floating-liquid-static dribble out the corners of your mouth.

From behind, you hear voices. First one, then dozens, then hundreds. Before long, there are an uncountable number, all cheering, all wailing, all crying, and all whispering the same name over and over again. "Ush-Tik-a! Ush-Tik-a!"

The voices give way to static. Your vision fades away too. An awareness comes over you. It's a wholly indescribable feeling. You hear the thoughts of hundreds of different people and feel the soil of a thousand different places— places on this planet and on innumerable others scattered across the cosmos. It's a cacophony of endless noise. A perfect contortion of sound, blended to make one, long venomous drawl.
As static overwhelms your being, you realize that each tiny speck looks like its own private little star. Your final thought is how beautiful they look.
Go to 354.
You flop onto the bed and stretch your legs. Charlie rewinds the tape, takes the VCR remote, then lays down next to you.
"Cozy?" "Yep," you say. "Alright. Wildcard movie is go." Charlie smiles, then hits play.
Go to 22.
You clamp your hands hard over your ears but somehow the static still seeps in. Charlie, next to you, does the same. Their lips are moving, but you can't tell what they're saying.
You yell something about the remote, but even your own voice is lost, hidden beneath the TV's digital wailing.

Charlie pulls one hand down and fiddles with the remote. The screeching continues. Charlie snarls, tosses the remote aside, then staggers over to the TV. You watch them go. The TV looks reflected somehow in the windows behind it. Pine trees stand guard on the Black Hills outside, but they're riddled with static. Riddled with static. Static. STATIC!
You clamp your eyes shut. Charlie turns the dial on the TV and kills the noise. The screen goes black. A blaring ring lingers a little in your ears.
"What in the hell was that?" you ask. Charlie catches their breath for a moment, then shrugs. "I dunno..."
"How the hell was it so damn loud?" "Top of the range speakers?" You roll your eyes. "Great. At least there's a top TV to watch a creepy peeping Tom video on."
"Oh, c'mon. That wasn't a peeping Tom." Charlie gestures to the TV cabinet. "Why would Mark and Julie have the tape?"
If Broken Heart is checked on the log sheet, you cannot stay calm. You must go to 24.
To get frustrated with Charlie, go to 24. To stay calm, go to 30.
You shake your head and take a deep breath. "You're right. It's stupid. Let's just forget about… whatever the hell that was."

"You still wanna watch a movie?" Charlie asks. "Sure. Whatever is fine. One of those schlocky flicks…," you say. Charlie gets up. "My pick?" "Your pick." Charlie smiles and looks over the tapes in the cabinet. "Ooh! This is a good one." You lean forward to look at a tape that has a guy wearing a pumpkin on his head as the cover. "I think even you'll like it, babe."

"Somehow, I doubt it." You smile. "No, seriously," Charlie says, and slips the tape from the case. "It's about this guy who's a writer, and he drives up to this secluded town in Maine, right?" Charlie hits eject on the VCR. "And anyway, when he—"
The TV set blares to life. It bellows static through the cabin. Thunderous scraping and coughing bounces off the walls.

You thrash and cover your ears. Charlie swears but you can hardly hear it. The noise builds to a frenetic peak. It's almost unbearable. Then, just as quick as it began, the noise stops, and the TV falls silent. All the lights in the cabin go dead. The power is out.
Go to 31.
"Charlie?" you ask the darkness.
"Yeah?" "What was that?" "Power's out, I think." You hear scrambling in the darkness as Charlie shuffles along the floor, one hand touching the wall. They flick the light switch several times.
"I thought this place was on solar power?" "Well, I guess solar power still runs out." "Is there a back-up or anything?" "I dunno. I guess I'll have to head into town and call Mark in the morning."
"Oh, that's just great." You pull your legs to your chest. "Okay, whatever."
You're not used to this level of dark. The city doesn't get dark like this. You raise your hand in front of your face. You can't even see its outline. You feel anxiety rising in your chest.
If either Broken Heart or Blame Game is checked/ticked on the log sheet, you cannot lean on Charlie for support. You must go to 33.
To lean on Charlie for support, go to 32. To give up and go to sleep, go to 33.
"Charlie, can you come to bed?"

"Sure." The bedframe creaks as Charlie crawls onto it. In the silence following the outburst from the TV, even the slightest sound rings deafeningly loud in the quiet. You feel Charlie cuddle up close to you.
"I'm sorry," Charlie says. "Don't be."
"Must just be an old shoddy set. I think Mark has had it since the 80s. We'll fix it tomorrow."

You murmur softly in agreement. Charlie wraps an arm around you. You feel their breathing on the back of your neck. It slows quickly and soon fades into the gentle rumble of sleep. The sound is steady and calming. Before long, you drift off, too. The only sound that disturbs you is the faint creaking of pines echoing softly through the Black Hills.
Go to 34.
This cabin sucks. You shift around on the lumpy bed and try to get comfortable. Charlie joins you before long. The bedframe creaks when they settle onto it.
"…Babe?" Charlie says. "What?" "Are you going to sleep?" "What else am I supposed to do? The power is out and we're in the middle of the woods."
"Okay, sorry." Charlie rolls over. At least you think they do. It's hard to tell in the dark. After a few moments, they speak again.
"Must just be an old shoddy TV. I think Mark has had it since the 80s."
"I don't care. Can we just make sure the power is back tomorrow?"

"Yeah. I'll do everything I can." "Fine. Goodnight then," you say. "Goodnight." Charlie doesn't stay awake long. You hear their breathing slow quickly and fade into the gentle rumble of sleep. For you, sleep comes much later. The creaking of pines, the howl of cold wind, and other strange and unidentifiable sounds echo through the Black Hills around you. The anxiety in your chest burns as you lie silently in the dark. It's a relief when you finally fall asleep.
Check/tick Nyctophobe on the log sheet. Go to 34.
When you wake in the morning you are alone.
You stir in the bed and sit up. "Babe?"

There's no answer. The only sound is the wind outside, carrying with it a gentle morning birdsong. You get up and cross to the kitchen. There's a note taped to the chunky refrigerator, which is written in familiar handwriting:
"Sorry again. Just want this weekend to be special. Gone to town to get help fixing power. Back ASAP. Love you."
You set the note down. Looks like you have a few hours to yourself.
To eat some breakfast, go to 35. To go for a brisk walk, go to 37.

You scrounge up some bacon and eggs. The spit and splutter of cooking fat fills the kitchen. The leaden quiet out here is unsettling. More than once you make to turn the radio on before remembering that it won't work with the power out. You poke at your eggs idly with a spatula and slowly run your eyes across the room. They land on the dormant television set. Your heartbeat quickens.
You frown. It's embarrassing how much that stupid video tape affected you. You roll your eyes and turn off the gas.
You eat your hearty breakfast in silence. Once you're done and have washed the dishes, you realize you've got nothing else to do, so decide to go for a walk.
To leave right away, go to 36. To wait a few minutes in case your partner returns, go to 41.

Outside, the air is fresh, the sun is warm, and the sky is mostly clear. You fill your lungs with the scent of moist soil and pine trees. You take a few steps forward and peer down the driveway. It weaves away into the woods. The trees are so thick here that you'd probably have a better chance listening out for cars than looking for them.
You turn and head down a walking trail just by the cabin. The earth has been worn smooth by the hiking shoes of innumerable visiting families.
To slowly get excited about this vacation, go to 39. To grow even more anxious, go to 40.

Outside, the air is fresh, the sun is warm, and the sky is mostly clear. You fill your lungs with the scent of moist soil and pine trees. You take a few steps forward and peer down the driveway. It weaves away into the woods. The trees are so thick here that you'd probably have a better chance listening out for cars than looking for them.
You turn and head down a walking trail just by the cabin. The earth has been worn smooth by the hiking shoes of innumerable visiting families.
The forest grows thicker around you as you walk. Unseen critters skitter past in the underbrush. Birds move through the branches above, calling out and making pine needles rustle.
You come across a blueberry bush just by the trail.
To stop and collect berries, go to 38. To continue your walk, go to 39.
You squat down and pick berries from the bush. Their flesh is weak. Juices spill off and stain your fingers purple. You're
about to lick them clean when you hesitate. Blueberries are safe to eat, right? It wouldn't be a good look to accidentally poison yourself the first time you set foot outside the cabin.
Make a Natural World roll: • If you succeed the roll, go to 77. • If you fail the roll, go to 104.

The nature surrounding you eats away at the stress layered into your being. You feel yourself truly smile for the first time in weeks. It happens without any effort on your part. It feels good. You close your eyes and turn your face to the sky. The fresh air and sunlight kiss your skin. It's glorious.
Off to the left, you hear running water. You open your eyes and look towards the source of the sound. It's coming from just off the trail you've been walking along.
